source_batch.unit_label: Module A: International Banking - Facilities for Exporters and Importers

facts.statement: The period of a rupee packing credit advance is decided by the bank case by case, on the time needed to procure, manufacture or process and ship the goods or render the services. If pre-shipment advances are not adjusted by submission of export documents within 360 days from the date of advance, they cease to qualify as export credit ab initio. If exports do not materialise at all, the bank charges on the packing credit the domestic lending rate plus any penal charges set under a Board-approved transparent policy. Each packing credit is generally kept as a separate account to monitor period and end-use.

Packing credit is liquidated from the proceeds of bills drawn for the exported goods on purchase or discount, which converts the pre-shipment credit into post-shipment credit; by mutual agreement it may also be repaid from EEFC balances and from the exporter's rupee resources to the extent exports have actually taken place. For exporters with a good track record the bank may allow liquidation from export documents of another order or commodity (substitution of contract) where commercially necessary and unavoidable, and may mark off packing credit with proceeds of documents on which no packing credit was drawn after checking another bank did not give packing credit; these relaxations are not extended to sister, associate or group concerns.

A bank may extend a pre-shipment credit running account facility without prior lodgement of letters of credit or firm orders, in anticipation of orders, only to exporters with a good track record and to EOUs and units in free trade zones, export processing zones and SEZs; letters of credit or orders must be produced within a reasonable period; export bills are marked off against the earliest outstanding pre-shipment credit on a first-in-first-out basis, never beyond the sanctioned period or 360 days from the date of advance; the facility is withdrawn if misused and is not given to sub-suppliers.

For rupee post-shipment credit on demand bills the period of advance is the Normal Transit Period (NTP) specified by FEDAI; for usance bills credit is granted for a maximum of 365 days from the date of shipment, inclusive of NTP and grace period, if any, and the bank must monitor the need for extension and persuade exporters to realise the proceeds in a shorter period. Adjusted bills continue to be followed up for realisation and reported in EDPMS, and an exporter with overdue bills may extinguish the overdue post-shipment credit from rupee resources while the EDF remains outstanding.

Where exporters draw bills for 90 to 98 per cent of the FOB value and the residual undrawn balance is payable by the overseas buyer after checking quality or quantity, payment of the undrawn balance is contingent, and the bank may grant advances against it on commercial judgement and the buyer's track record.

Authorised dealers may extend pre-shipment credit in foreign currency (PCFC) to exporters for domestic and imported inputs, at interest set by the bank on a widely accepted Alternative Reference Rate in the currency concerned under its Board-approved policy. PCFC applies only to cash exports; may be in any convertible currency, including a different currency from the invoice (the cross-currency risk is the exporter's) and for exports to ACU countries; is funded from EEFC, RFC(D) and FCNR(B) balances, escrow accounts, lines of credit from overseas banks, or swaps; if the exporter has supplier's credit for imported inputs, PCFC finances only domestic inputs; and is available for a maximum of 360 days.

Under the Export Bills Rediscounting (EBR) scheme, post-shipment credit in foreign currency covers mainly usance export bills of up to 180 days from the date of shipment, inclusive of normal transit period and grace, and may go beyond 180 days if the borrower is entitled to draw longer usance; it may be offered in any convertible currency and for exports to ACU countries. Bills rediscounted abroad with recourse count for export credit performance; bills rediscounted without recourse do not.

Each bank lays down criteria for Gold Cards for creditworthy exporters with a good track record, including MSMEs. The scheme does not apply to exporters on ECGC's Specific Approval List or with overdue bills above 10 per cent of the previous year's turnover. Gold Card holders get better terms than other exporters, including interest not above the bank's general export credit rate; simpler and faster processing; lower fees; in-principle limits for three years with automatic renewal; a stand-by limit of not less than 20 per cent of the assessed limit; relaxed inventory norms for unanticipated orders; requests processed within 25 days for fresh applications, 15 days for renewals and seven days for ad hoc limits; preference in PCFC; and possible waiver of collateral and of ECGC ECIB schemes.

The courseware (S03 printed pp. 138-147) describes packing credit with a normal total period of 180 days extendable to 360 days, a 13-14% (sea) or 25% (air) deduction to reach FOB value, interest linked to the MCLR from 1 April 2016, and foreign currency export credit at LIBOR-linked rates with a note that LIBOR is replaced by SOFR or another ARR; its sanction illustration uses MCLR-linked rates.

payload.title: Rupee packing credit today: the 360-day rule, not the 180-day rule
payload.core_explanation_md:
Older books say a packing credit should not exceed **180 days** and may stretch to **360**. RBI's consolidated directions (Chapter XV, from November 2025) say it differently.

- **Period**: the **bank decides** it, case by case, based on the time to procure, make and ship.
- **The hard stop**: if the advance is not **adjusted by export documents within 360 days** of the advance, it **stops qualifying as export credit, from the start (ab initio)**.
- **If no export happens at all**: the bank charges the **domestic lending rate plus any penal charges** under a Board-approved policy.
- **Separate account** for each packing credit, to watch period and end-use.
- **Rate**: banks follow RBI's interest-rate directions, not the old **MCLR** rule of April 2016 in the courseware.

payload.title: Paying off packing credit: bills first, flexibility for the trusted
payload.core_explanation_md:
**The normal route**: the packing credit is **liquidated from the proceeds of the export bills** on purchase or discount. This **converts pre-shipment credit into post-shipment credit**.

**Other sources, by agreement**: balances in the **EEFC account**, and the exporter's **rupee resources** to the extent exports have actually taken place.

**Relaxations for good track records**
- **Substitution of contract**: liquidate from documents of **another order or commodity**, where it is **commercially necessary and unavoidable**.
- **Mark off** packing credit with proceeds of documents on which **no packing credit** was drawn, after checking **no other bank** gave packing credit for them.

**Never** for **sister, associate or group concerns**.

payload.title: The running account: packing credit before the order arrives
payload.core_explanation_md:
Normally a bank lends against a **firm order or letter of credit**. Where raw materials are **seasonal**, or manufacture takes longer than the delivery schedule, it may extend a **running account** and lend **before the order is in hand**.

**Who**: exporters with a **good track record**, and **EOUs and units in free trade zones, export processing zones and SEZs**. **Not sub-suppliers**.

**Conditions**
- The **order or LC must be produced within a reasonable time**.
- Export bills are marked off against the **earliest outstanding advance, first in first out**, within the **sanctioned period or 360 days**, whichever is earlier.
- **Misuse** means the facility is withdrawn at once; non-compliance means the advance is **not export credit ab initio**.

payload.title: After shipment: how long, and what about the undrawn balance?
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Demand bills**: credit runs for the **Normal Transit Period (NTP)**, a period fixed by **FEDAI**.

**Usance bills**: credit for **at most 365 days from the shipment date**, **including** the NTP and any grace period. The bank must **monitor the need** for the full period and **press exporters to realise early**.

**Overdue bills**: an exporter may clear overdue post-shipment credit from **rupee resources** to cut the interest cost, but the **EDF stays outstanding** and the bill is **still followed up** and reported in **EDPMS**.

**Undrawn balance**: in some trades the bill is drawn for only **90 to 98%** of FOB, the rest paid after the buyer checks quality or quantity. That balance is **contingent**, so the bank may lend against it on **commercial judgement** and the **buyer's record**.

payload.title: Export credit in foreign currency: PCFC and EBR
payload.core_explanation_md:
**PCFC (pre-shipment credit in foreign currency)**
- For **domestic and imported inputs**, at a rate the bank sets using a widely accepted **Alternative Reference Rate (ARR)** (LIBOR has gone).
- **Cash exports only**; any **convertible currency**, even one different from the invoice (the **cross-currency risk is the exporter's**); **ACU** exports included.
- Funded from **EEFC, RFC(D), FCNR(B)** balances, escrow accounts, overseas lines of credit, or **swaps**.
- If the exporter has **supplier's credit** for imported inputs, PCFC covers **domestic inputs only**.
- **Maximum 360 days**.

**EBR (export bills rediscounted)**
- Post-shipment credit in foreign currency, normally for **usance bills up to 180 days** from shipment, inclusive of transit and grace; longer if the borrower may draw longer usance.
- Bills rediscounted abroad **with recourse** count for export credit performance; **without recourse** do not.

payload.title: The Gold Card: fewer hurdles for exporters with a good record
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Who gets one**: creditworthy exporters with a **good track record**, MSMEs included, on **criteria each bank sets**. **Not** exporters on ECGC's **Specific Approval List**, or with **overdue bills above 10% of the previous year's turnover**.

**What holders get**
- **Better terms**, with interest **not above the bank's general export credit rate**.
- **Simpler, faster processing**: fresh applications in **25 days**, renewals in **15 days**, ad hoc limits in **7 days**.
- **In-principle limits for three years**, with automatic renewal.
- A **stand-by limit of at least 20% of the assessed limit** for sudden orders.
- **Relaxed inventory norms** for unanticipated orders.
- **Preference in PCFC**, lower fees, and possible **waiver of collateral** and ECGC ECIB cover.

payload.title: Two quick calculations: the usance credit deadline and the Gold Card stand-by limit
payload.core_explanation_md: Illustrative case: goods are shipped on 1 February 2026 under a usance bill, and the bank grants post-shipment credit for the maximum period. Separately, a Gold Card exporter has an assessed limit of ₹42,00,00,000 (₹42 crore). What is the last date of the post-shipment credit, and what is the minimum stand-by limit?

worked_steps.description: Maximum period for usance post-shipment credit, counted from shipment and including transit and grace.
Minimum stand-by limit: 20% of the assessed limit.

payload.final_answer_with_unit: The credit can run to 1 February 2027; the stand-by limit must be at least ₹8,40,00,000.00

self_check.expected_takeaway: Only for the Normal Transit Period set by FEDAI, not 365 days.

payload.stem_md: A Gold Card exporter's assessed limit is ₹36,50,00,000. What is the minimum stand-by limit the bank must make additionally available, in rupees?

numeric_rule.rounding_instruction: Give the answer to 2 decimal places.

payload.correct_explanation_md: The stand-by limit is not less than 20% of the assessed limit: 36,50,00,000 × 20% = ₹7,30,00,000.00.

options.explanation_md: The relaxations are not extended to sister, associate or group concerns.

options.text_md: Writing it off against export incentives
options.explanation_md: No such relaxation exists.

options.text_md: Liquidating it from export documents of another order, where this is commercially necessary and unavoidable

options.text_md: Sub-suppliers of the export order holder
options.explanation_md: It is not granted to sub-suppliers.

options.explanation_md: Eligibility is limited.

options.text_md: Exporters with a good track record, and EOUs and units in free trade zones, export processing zones or SEZs
options.explanation_md: These are the eligible categories.

options.explanation_md: The Gold Card is a separate scheme.

payload.stem_md: What is the maximum period of rupee post-shipment credit for a usance bill?

options.text_md: 365 days from the date of shipment, inclusive of normal transit period and grace period
options.explanation_md: This is the stated maximum.

options.text_md: 180 days from the date of shipment
options.explanation_md: That was the older limit, and it is the EBR norm for foreign currency.

options.text_md: The normal transit period only
options.explanation_md: That applies to demand bills.

options.text_md: 90 days from the date of acceptance
options.explanation_md: No such limit applies.

payload.correct_explanation_md: Credit for usance bills is granted for a maximum of 365 days from the date of shipment, inclusive of NTP and grace.

payload.stem_md: Which statement about pre-shipment credit in foreign currency (PCFC) is correct?

options.text_md: Its interest rate is fixed by RBI at LIBOR plus 1%
options.explanation_md: Banks use a widely accepted ARR under Board-approved policy.

options.text_md: It is available for a maximum of 360 days and applies only to cash exports
options.explanation_md: Both points are stated.

options.text_md: It must be in the same currency as the invoice
options.explanation_md: It may be in another convertible currency at the exporter's cross-currency risk.

options.text_md: It finances imported inputs even if supplier's credit exists
options.explanation_md: With supplier's credit, PCFC finances domestic inputs only.

payload.correct_explanation_md: PCFC applies only to cash exports and is available for a maximum of 360 days; the rate uses an ARR and the currency may differ from the invoice.

payload.stem_md: Bills rediscounted abroad under the EBR scheme: which count towards export credit performance?

options.text_md: Bills rediscounted abroad without recourse
options.explanation_md: Bills rediscounted without recourse do not count.

options.text_md: Both kinds count equally
options.explanation_md: The two kinds are not treated equally.

options.text_md: Bills rediscounted abroad with recourse
options.explanation_md: Bills rediscounted abroad with recourse count towards export credit performance.

options.text_md: Neither kind counts
options.explanation_md: Some rediscounted bills do count.

payload.correct_explanation_md: Bills rediscounted abroad with recourse count towards export credit performance.

payload.stem_md: Which exporter is NOT eligible for a Gold Card?

options.text_md: An MSME exporter with a good track record
options.explanation_md: An MSME exporter with a good record can be eligible.

options.text_md: A creditworthy exporter that meets the bank's criteria
options.explanation_md: A creditworthy exporter meeting the bank's criteria can be eligible.

options.text_md: An exporter that wants a stand-by limit
options.explanation_md: Wanting a stand-by limit is the purpose of the card.

options.text_md: One with overdue bills above 10% of the previous year's turnover
options.explanation_md: An exporter with overdue bills above 10 per cent of the previous year's turnover is not eligible for a Gold Card.

payload.correct_explanation_md: An exporter with overdue bills above 10 per cent of the previous year's turnover is not eligible for a Gold Card.

payload.stem_md: Within how many days must a bank process a fresh application for a limit from a Gold Card holder?

options.text_md: 25 days
options.explanation_md: Fresh applications are processed within 25 days; renewals 15 and ad hoc limits 7.

options.text_md: 15 days
options.explanation_md: That is for renewals of limits.

options.text_md: 7 days
options.explanation_md: That is for ad hoc limits.

options.text_md: 60 days
options.explanation_md: No such period applies.

payload.correct_explanation_md: Requests from Gold Card holders are processed within 25 days for fresh applications, 15 days for renewals and seven days for ad hoc limits.

payload.stem_md: Goods are shipped on 1 February 2026 under a usance bill. What is the last day of rupee post-shipment credit at the maximum period?

options.text_md: 1 August 2026
options.explanation_md: 1 August 2026 is only six months.

options.text_md: 1 February 2027
options.explanation_md: Maximum rupee post-shipment credit for a usance bill shipped on 1 February 2026 ends on 1 February 2027.

options.text_md: 2 February 2027
options.explanation_md: 2 February 2027 is one day beyond.

options.text_md: 31 January 2027
options.explanation_md: 31 January 2027 is one day short.

payload.correct_explanation_md: Maximum rupee post-shipment credit for a usance bill shipped on 1 February 2026 ends on 1 February 2027.

unresolved: The saved page of RBI's Credit Facilities Directions is the version updated on 1 October 2026, after the 30 June 2026 cut-off; the Directions of 28 November 2025 were in force at the cut-off, but earlier versions of Chapter XV were not retrieved.

The courseware's 180-day packing credit period, 13-14% and 25% deductions to reach FOB value, MCLR linkage, LIBOR-linked foreign currency rates and its sanction illustration (printed pp. 138-147) are superseded or bank-specific and are not taught; the card flags the difference.
The Normal Transit Period of 25 days (courseware printed p. 143) is a FEDAI rule that was not retrieved; the Directions say NTP is as specified by FEDAI, and no item states a number of days.
The courseware's concessional-interest periods and 90-day advance against undrawn balances differ from the Directions (commercial judgement); the Directions are taught.
Crystallisation of overdue export bills (printed p. 144) is a FEDAI rule and is not taught.
RBI's Trade Relief Measures Directions (extended credit period for eligible accounts) are not taught.
Reviewer for this batch is the authoring agent; no independent or human review.

items.stem_md: Which statement about pre-shipment credit in foreign currency (PCFC) is correct?

options.text_md: Its interest rate is fixed by RBI at LIBOR plus 1%
options.explanation_md: Banks use a widely accepted ARR under Board-approved policy.

options.text_md: It is available for a maximum of 360 days and applies only to cash exports
options.explanation_md: Both points are stated.

options.text_md: It must be in the same currency as the invoice
options.explanation_md: It may be in another convertible currency at the exporter's cross-currency risk.

options.text_md: It finances imported inputs even if supplier's credit exists
options.explanation_md: With supplier's credit, PCFC finances domestic inputs only.

items.correct_explanation_md: PCFC applies only to cash exports and is available for a maximum of 360 days; the rate uses an ARR and the currency may differ from the invoice.
